paragraphs.text: Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia type III (FHH3) is an autosomal dominant disorder of extracellular calcium homeostasis. Nesbit et al. (2013) noted that FHH1 and FHH2 usually have normal circulating PTH and are generally asymptomatic. In contrast, FHH3 is characterized by increased serum PTH concentrations, hypophosphatemia, and osteomalacia. Howles et al. (2016) described FHH3 as the most clinically severe of the 3 types of familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia. They stated that it is caused by heterozygous AP2S1 mutations resulting in Arg15Cys, Arg15His, or Arg15Leu substitutions, and that the mutant AP2-sigma proteins impair signal transduction mediated by the calcium-sensing receptor.

paragraphs.text: McMurtry et al. (1992) studied a large kindred with familial benign (hypocalciuric) hypercalcemia. After the proposita was identified, they surveyed 46 kindred members from 5 generations, aged 1.5 to 91 years, biochemically and/or by chart review. Of these, 19 were affected. Fifteen hypercalcemic subjects were examined biochemically, and their serum immunoreactive PTH levels, measured in 3 separate immunoassays, became supranormal by about age 30 years and appeared to rise further thereafter. Affected members had lower serum inorganic phosphate than unaffected members, with normal serum alkaline phosphatase activity and normal serum creatinine. Five affected adults older than 40 years were studied radiographically, and 3 of them had changes suggestive of osteomalacia. In one of these, a 51-year-old woman, iliac crest biopsy confirmed defective skeletal mineralization. McMurtry et al. (1992) concluded that the disorder in this kindred may not be totally benign, because osteomalacia can develop in adulthood, perhaps due to mild hypophosphatemia. They suggested that it might be an unusual variant of familial benign hypercalcemia.

paragraphs.text: In the Oklahoma kindred, Hannan et al. (2010) found linkage to 10 of 14 informative 19q13 microsatellite loci, with a maximum 2-point lod score of 6.92 at theta = 0 for D19S606. The syntenic region on mouse chromosome 7 contains 4 Casr-related sequences (Gprc2a-rs1, -rs2, -rs3, and -rs5), but no human or primate homologs of these were present in the human interval. Comparative analysis showed that 2 conserved segments were inverted between mouse and human, and that an 11.6-Mb mouse region containing 35 genes, including the 4 Gprc2a-rs genes, was absent from the human genome. The authors concluded that FBHH3 could not be attributed to Gprc2a-rs defects.

paragraphs.text: From the AP2 crystal structure, Nesbit et al. (2013) noted that Arg15 of AP2-sigma-2 is conserved in all orthologs and in the human AP sigma paralogs. Together with Arg21 of AP2-alpha-1, it forms key contacts with the glutamine at position -4 of the dileucine motif of cargo proteins, and substitution by Cys or Leu was predicted to reduce affinity for this motif. Mutating the C-terminal dileucine motif of CaSR (Leu-Leu1013-1014 to Ala-Ala) in transfected HEK293 cells shifted the calcium concentration-response curve to the right with a significantly higher EC50, indicating that the motif is functionally significant. In an intact-cell ELISA, cells transfected with wildtype AP2S1 showed a further reduction in cell-surface CaSR after stimulation with high extracellular calcium, compared with cells transfected with the R15C mutant or with vector. This indicated that AP2-sigma-2 has a role in CaSR endocytosis that is disrupted by the Arg15 mutants. Nesbit et al. (2013) noted that although AP2-sigma-2 is ubiquitously expressed, Arg15 mutations cause a specific disorder of extracellular calcium homeostasis rather than a multisystem disorder. They suggested that this may be because Arg15 has a specific role, such as recognizing the CaSR dileucine motif.
